Launch-window laboratory

Find the moment when Earth, Mars, and a spacecraft can meet.

This app converts the workbook into a working student laboratory: derive the Hohmann transfer, compare the circular-orbit phase angle with a DE421 variable-speed Mars reference, inspect ΔV and time-of-flight, find real planetary alignments, and animate the journey.

1.00 AUEarth mean orbit
1.52 AUMars mean orbit
≈44.65°circular-orbit phase baseline

1. Build the transfer

Use the mean Earth–Sun and Mars–Sun distances to calculate the Hohmann ellipse semi-major axis and orbital period.

2. Find Mars at launch

During the spacecraft’s half-orbit, Mars keeps moving. Subtract that motion from 180° to obtain the required lead angle.

3. Replace the circular cartoon

Load DE421 to evaluate JPL Chebyshev ephemerides in-browser and search actual Earth–Mars heliocentric phase geometry.

Walter Hohmann

Hohmann’s two-impulse transfer provides the classic minimum-energy transfer between two coplanar circular orbits. The workbook’s Earth→Mars exercise is built around half of this transfer ellipse.

Student Worksheet

Nine checked calculations reproduce the workbook’s core launch-window derivation using the 0.10 AU measurement grid.

Classroom model: 1 AU = 149,600,000 km, 1 grid square = 0.10 AU, Earth = 1.00 AU, Mars = 1.52 AU, Earth year = 365.25 d, Mars year = 687 d. The orbital radii used by the worksheet are derived from the grid measurement below.

Workshop measurement diagram

Count radial grid squares from the Sun. Use the scale consistently in Steps 1–2 and all calculations that follow.

1 square = 0.10 AU
Measure from the centre of the Sun to the orbital radius. Earth is 10.0 squares from the Sun → 1.00 AU. Mars is 15.2 squares from the Sun → 1.52 AU. These measured values feed the transfer semi-major axis, period, time of flight and launch phase-angle calculations.
1

Earth–Sun distance from the 0.10 AU grid

From the measurement diagram, Earth’s orbital radius is 10.0 grid squares. Each square represents 0.10 AU. Calculate rEarth.

10.0 squares × 0.10 AU/square = ?
AU
Multiply 10.0 by 0.10 AU per square. The result should match Earth’s familiar orbital radius of about 1 AU.
2

Mars–Sun distance from the 0.10 AU grid

From the same measurement diagram, Mars’s orbital radius is 15.2 grid squares. Each square represents 0.10 AU. Calculate rMars.

15.2 squares × 0.10 AU/square = ?
AU
Multiply 15.2 by 0.10 AU per square. The result should be a little more than 1.5 AU.
3

Convert Mars distance to kilometres

Use your Mars distance and 1 AU = 149,600,000 km.

rMars = 1.52 × 149,600,000 km
km
Keep all digits from the multiplication; you can enter 227392000.
4

Hohmann transfer semi-major axis

The transfer ellipse touches Earth at perihelion and Mars at aphelion.

at = (rE + rM) / 2
AUkm
Average the two orbital radii: (1.00 + 1.52)/2.
5

Orbital period of the transfer ellipse

Using years and AU, Kepler’s third law becomes P² = a³.

P = √(a³)
yearsdays
First calculate 1.26³, then take the square root, then multiply by 365.25.
6

Travel time to Mars

The spacecraft travels half of the transfer ellipse.

TOF = Ptransfer / 2
days
Your answer should be about 8.5 months.
7

How many degrees does Mars travel per day?

The classroom model uses a Mars orbital period of 687 days.

ωMars = 360° / 687 d
°/day
It is slightly more than half a degree per day.
8

How far does Mars move during the spacecraft flight?

Multiply Mars’s daily angular motion by the time of flight.

ΔθMars = TOF × ωMars
degrees
Use your answers from steps 6 and 7.
9

Required Mars lead angle at launch

The spacecraft reaches the opposite side of the Sun, 180° from launch. Mars must move into that arrival point while the spacecraft is in flight.

φ = 180° − ΔθMars
degrees ahead of Earth
The workbook rounds this to about 44°. With full precision it is close to 44.65°.

A planetary phase-angle crossing is not the same as an operational launch window. Real mission windows also depend on launch-site geometry, launch vehicle capability, C3, arrival conditions, navigation, planetary protection, and mission-specific constraints.

Mission Design Activity

Preserves the workbook’s “find four solutions and refine” exercise, while separating it from the ideal Hohmann calculation.

Workbook activity constraints: mission duration 111–321 days and trajectory-browser total ΔV 7–10 km/s. That “total ΔV” is not identical to the ideal heliocentric Hohmann ΔV in the Physics tab, so the two numbers should not be compared as if they were the same metric.
SolutionDepartureArrivalDuration (d)Total ΔV (km/s)RouteConstraint check

Trajectory quantities in the workbook

C3 is characteristic energy, equal to v∞² for Earth escape. The workbook also introduces launch asymptote declination (DLA), injection ΔV, post-injection ΔV, and total ΔV as quantities used to compare mission trajectories.

Student task

Enter or import four candidate solutions. Try to satisfy the workbook limits. Then compare the candidates with the low-energy Hohmann baseline and discuss why a real trajectory can depart from the simple circular model.

Transfer Physics

Correct two-body Hohmann equations for the quantities developed across the workbook sheets.

Core equations

a = (r₁+r₂)/2

P = 2π√(a³/μ☉)

v = √[ μ☉(2/r − 1/a) ]

TOF = P/2

Velocity changes

The app intentionally corrects inconsistent velocity-transfer formulas found in the original workbook. In a two-body Hohmann transfer, the transfer-orbit speeds are computed with the vis-viva equation, then ΔV is the difference between circular-orbit and transfer-orbit speeds at each tangent point.
